Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 72, verses 11–15:

(p-432) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that; we were of divergent ways.﴾ ﴿And we thought that we would never cause Allah to fail on the earth, nor would we escape Him by flight.﴾ ﴿And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it. Whoever believes in his Lord fears neither a diminution [of his reward] nor an increase [of his burden].﴾ ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators. Whoever submits, those have sought out right guidance.﴾ ﴿But as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾

All of this is the speech of the jinn, up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ As for His saying, "and among us are those below that," it means: other than the righteous. It is as if they said: "Among us are a people or a group below the righteous." This is a phrase that sometimes takes the place of "ghayr" (other than). "Al-tara'iq" means differing paths, and "al-qidad" likewise means differing things, as if [each] had been separated from the others and distinguished. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Qatada said: "tara'iqa qidadan" means divergent desires. Others said: divergent groups. Al-Kumayt said:

I gathered with my opinion from them every sect of rejectors,
when they were divergent paths in their desires, separated.

Their saying, "and we thought that we would never cause Allah to fail," here "thought" (zann) means knowledge. This is their report about their state after their belief in what they heard from Muhammad (ﷺ). By "guidance" they mean the Qur'an; they called it guidance because it is the cause of guidance. "Al-bakhs" is the diminishing of good deeds, and "al-rahaq" is the increase in evil deeds. Al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read "fala yakhaf" with a jussive (sukun) and without an alif.

After this, Allah the Exalted divided the state of people in the Hereafter in the manner in which the speaker among the jinn had divided. So His saying: ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators.﴾ "Al-qasit" means the wrongdoer, as said by Mujahid, Qatada and the people, and from it is the saying of the poet:

A people who killed the son of Hind by force,
... 'Amr, and they transgressed against al-Nu'man.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 72, verses 16–22:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿And if they had remained steadfast upon the Way, We would have given them abundant water to drink.﴾ ﴿That We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah.﴾ ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him, they nearly became a crowd against him.﴾ ﴿Say: "I only invoke my Lord and I associate no one with Him."﴾ ﴿Say: "I possess no harm for you, nor any guidance."﴾ ﴿Say: "No one will protect me from Allah, nor will I find any refuge besides Him."﴾

The pronoun (dhamir) in His saying "istaqamu" (they remained steadfast). Abu Mijlaz, al-Farra', al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and al-Dahhak (in one of the reports from him) said: it refers to His saying "man aslama" (whoever submitted). "The Way" is the way of disbelief. The meaning is: if those among the people who had submitted had disbelieved, We would have given them water, as a respite for them and a gradual drawing-in (istidraj). Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid said: the pronoun refers to "al-qasitin" (the deviators), and the meaning is: upon the way of Islam and truth. This meaning is like His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have absolved them of their misdeeds﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 65], and His saying: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 66]. This view is clearer, because using "istiqama" (steadfastness) for disbelief is strained.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wuthab recited "wa-an law istaqamu" with a ḍamma on the waw. Abu al-Fath said: this is a likening to the waw of the plural (waw al-jama'a), as in ﴿They bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqara: 16]. "Al-maʼ al-ghadaq" means abundant water. The majority of readers recited "ghadaqan" with a fatha on the dal. 'Asim, in al-A'mash's transmission from him, recited it with a kasra.

His saying "li-naftinahum fihi" (that We might test them therein): if the referent is the Muslims, its meaning is "li-nakhtabirahum" (that We might test them). If the referent is the deviators, its meaning is "li-namtahinahum wa-nastadrijahum" (that We might try them and draw them in gradually). 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Wherever the water is, there is the wealth, and wherever the wealth is, there is the trial," and he drew evidence from this verse. Al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyib, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) said: the Companions were obedient and attentive; then when the treasures of Khosrow and Caesar were conquered, (some) struck 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and he was killed, and the trials erupted.

"Yaslukhu" means "yadkhuluhu" (he will cause him to enter). 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited "yaslukhu" with a fatha on the ya', meaning "yaslukuhu Allah" (Allah will make him enter). Some of the Successors recited "yuslikhu" with a ḍamma on the ya', from aslaka, and both have the same meaning. The rest of the seven readers recited "nasluku" with the "plural of majesty" nun (nun al-'azama). Ibn Jubayr recited "naslukuhu" with a ḍamma on the nun and a kasra on the lam.

"Ṣa'adan" means "shaqqan" (arduous). One says: "Fulan is in ṣa'ad from his affair," meaning in hardship, and "this matter makes me ascend (yata'addafuni)," meaning it makes me strained. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Nothing has strained me (tasa'addani) as much as the marriage sermon has strained me." Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "Sa'ad" is a mountain in the Fire. Some people recited "ṣuʻudan" with ḍamma on the ṣad and the 'ayn. The majority recited with fatha on both the ṣad and the 'ayn. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited with ḍamma on the ṣad and fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that there is no rest in it.

As for one who opened the alif in "wa-anna al-masajida lillah" (and that the mosques are for Allah), he makes it a conjunction (ʻatf) on His saying: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that it...﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. Sibawayh mentioned this. As for "al-masajid" (the mosques), it was said: it means the houses that are for worship and prayer in every religious community. Al-Hasan said: it means every place where one prostrates, whether or not it was specially designated for that, since the entire earth is a mosque for this community. It is also narrated that this verse was revealed because of the Quraysh's domination over the Ka'ba at that time. So it was said to Muhammad ﷺ: all places belong to Allah the Exalted, so worship Him wherever you are. Ibn 'Ata' said: "al-masajid" are the limbs upon which one prostrates; its singular is "masjad" with a fatha on the jim. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the verse was revealed because the jinn said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed addressing them, meaning: your worship is accepted wherever you are. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: the meaning of the verse is: "And because the mosques are for Allah, do not invoke (anyone)" — that is, for this reason. Likewise, according to him, "li-ilafi Quraysh... fal-ya'budu" (for the accustomed security of Quraysh... let them worship), and likewise, according to him, ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Anbiya': 92]. The specifically designated mosques are clearly established as belonging to Allah the Exalted, so it is valid to set them apart for prayer, supplication, the recitation of knowledge, and everything that is purely for Allah the Exalted. They should not be used for discussing worldly affairs, nor for trade, nor made into thoroughfares, and no share of them should be given to other than Allah. I once sat to judge between Muslims in the main mosque in al-Mirya, then I saw in it the bad manners of litigants, their shouting, their oaths, the wickedness of disputation, its harms, and the entry of women. I saw that the house should be kept free of these, so I ceased sitting there to issue rulings.

His saying: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him﴾ may be a statement from Allah the Exalted, and it may be a report about the jinn. Some readers recited it (as mentioned above) with a fatha on the alif, "wa-annahu," as a conjunction on His saying "annahu istama'a" (that it listened). In this recitation, "al-'abd" (the servant) is Nuh, according to some people, and the pronoun in "kadu" (they nearly) refers to the jinn. The meaning is that they nearly crowded upon him to listen to the Qur'an. Others recited "wa-innahu" with a kasra on the hamza, and "al-'abd" is Muhammad ﷺ. The pronoun in "kadu" may refer to the jinn according to the meaning we mentioned, and it may refer to the disbelievers of his people and the Arabs, in their gathering to reject his command. It is not sound that "al-'abd" is Nuh, peace be upon him, except through a strained interpretation that disrupts the structure of the verse.

Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning of the verse is that it is the speech of the jinn to their people, relating it. "Al-'abd" is Muhammad ﷺ. The pronoun in "kadu" refers to his Companions who obey him and follow him in prayer. So they are "libad" against him. "Al-lubad" means groups, likened to something matted, piled one upon another. From this is the saying of 'Abd ibn Manaf ibn Rub':

*They struck with six or four verses, until it was as if a locust, gathering all, had matted over them.*

He means the locust. He called it "jani" because it gathers all things completely. [And it is narrated as "jabi'" with a ba', because it collects things by eating them.]

Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of the seven readers recited "libadan" with a kasra on the lam, the plural of "lubda." Ibn 'Abbas said: "a'wanan" (helpers). Ibn 'Amir, in one transmission from him, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin recited "libadan" with a ḍamma on the lam and a light (unshaddah) ba' with a fatha. It is also a plural. It is narrated from al-Jahdari "lubudan" with ḍamma on both the lam and the ba'. Abu Raja' recited "libbadan" with a kasra on the lam and a shaddah on the fatha-ed ba'. Al-Jahdari and al-Hasan (in one transmission from each) recited "lubbadan" with a ḍamma on the lam and a shaddah on the ba'; it is the plural of "labid." If we take the pronoun to refer to the jinn, the meaning is that they crowded upon him to listen to the remembrance. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. If we take it to refer to the disbelievers, the meaning is that they conspired against him and turned toward his affair with denial and rejection. This is the interpretation of al-Hasan and Qatada. "Yad'uhu" means "ya'buduhu" (he worships Him).

Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "qala innama ad'u rabbi" (he said: I only invoke my Lord), and this is the reading of the majority of the seven. It is a plural (jam') that cannot be avoided. If we take the pronoun to refer to the jinn, the meaning is that they crowded upon him to listen to the remembrance. This is the interpretation of al-Hasan and Qatada. "Ad'u" means "a'budu" (I worship). The majority of the seven recited this, and this recitation supports that "al-'abd" is Nuh, peace be upon him. 'Asim, Hamza, Ayyub, and Abu 'Amr (in one transmission from him) recited "qala innama ad'u" (he said: I only invoke), and this supports that it is Muhammad ﷺ, though the possibility remains for both. The readers differed on the fatha and the sukun of the ya' in "rabbi" (my Lord).

Then the Exalted commanded Muhammad ﷺ to disavow power, and that he possesses no harm or guidance for anyone; rather, the whole matter belongs to Allah the Exalted. Al-A'raj recited "rushudan" with ḍamma on the ra' and the shin. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "I possess no error (ghayyan) for you, nor right guidance (rushdan)." His saying: ﴿besides Him﴾ means: from beside other than Him. "Al-multahad" is the refuge to which one inclines and leans. From it comes "al-ilhad" (deviation) and "al-mayl" (inclination), and from it comes "al-lahd," the niche dug toward one of the two sides of a grave.

His saying: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him﴾ may be a statement from Allah the Exalted, and it may be a report about the jinn. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 72, verses 23–28:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Except a message from God and His messages. And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised, they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.﴾ ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a term.﴾ ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not reveal His unseen to anyone,﴾ ﴿except to a messenger whom He has chosen. Indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards.﴾ ﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord. And He has encompassed what is with them and has enumerated everything in number.﴾

The people differed concerning His saying, "Except a message" (illa balaghan). Al-Hasan said, in substance: it is an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it). The meaning is: "No one will protect me from God, except a message; for if I convey it, He will show mercy to me through it." The "protection" attributed to the message is a metaphor, since it is the cause of God's protection and mercy. Some of the grammarians said: according to this meaning it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning is: "I will not find a refuge except a message," that is, something I incline to and hold fast to, namely that I convey and obey, and then God will protect me. Qatada said: the implied sense is, "I do not possess anything except conveying; as for faith or disbelief, I do not possess them." Some of the interpreters said: "illa" is taken as a separate (non-exceptive) particle, "lan" is a conditional particle, and "la" is a negation. It is as if he were saying: "And I will not find a refuge if I do not convey from God and His messages." The "min" in His saying, "min Allah," is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). His saying, "And whoever disobeys God," intends disbelief, as evidenced by the mention of eternal abiding (al-khulud). Talha and Ibn Musarrif read "fa-inna lahu" (with the ending "inna"), meaning: "so his recompense is that for him..."

His, the Exalted, saying: "Until, when they see" (hatta idha ra'aw). He expressed the verb in the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. His saying, "who is weaker" (man ad'afu), may have "man" in the nominative position, as an interrogative and subject, with "ad'afu" as its predicate. It may also be that "min" is in the accusative position, governed by His saying, "fa-sa-ya'lamuna" (they will know), with "ad'afu" as the predicate of an implied subject.

Then God, the Exalted, commanded him to disclaim knowledge of the unseen at the time of their punishment, which they were promised. "Al-amad" means the duration and the limit. "'Alim" (Knower) may be a substitute (badal) for "my Lord," or it may be the predicate of an implied subject, in a separate (qat') construction. As-Suddi read "'Alam" as a past-tense verb with the "ba'" in the accusative. Al-Hasan read "fa-la yazhar" with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', and "ahadun" in the nominative. His, the Exalted, saying, "except one whom He has chosen of a messenger" (illa mani ertada min rasul), means: "He reveals to him what He wills of that, which is a little of much." Then God places around that angelic messenger guards (hafadhah) and watchers (rusad) against Iblis and his party, of the jinn and of mankind.

His, the Exalted, saying: "That He may know" (li-ya'lam). Qatada said: its meaning is that Muhammad may know that the messengers have conveyed the messages of their Lord, and that they were guarded and protected from them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its meaning is that Muhammad may know that the guarding angels, the watchers who descend before him, namely Jibril, peace be upon him, and behind him, have conveyed the messages of their Lord. Mujahid said: "That he may know" means that whoever denied or rejected that the messengers had conveyed (the messages) will come to know it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This knowledge will not occur to them except in the Hereafter.

It has also been said: the meaning is that God may know His messengers as conveyors who have come into existence, because His knowledge, glory be to Him, of everything has already preceded. The majority read "li-ya'lama" with a fatha on the lam, meaning: "that God, the Exalted, may know." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, read "li-yu'lama" with a damma on the ya'. Abu Haywa read "risalata rabbihim" in the singular. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-uhita" in the passive voice (of what has no named agent). His, the Exalted, saying, "and He has enumerated everything in number" (wa-ahsa kulla shay'in 'adadan), means: everything is counted. His, the Exalted, saying, "that He may know that they have..." (li-ya'lama an qad) to the end of the verse, implies that He, the Exalted, already knew that. On this implied verb, the words "ahata" and "ahsa" are coordinated.

And God, the Exalted, is the Guide, by His bounty and generosity.

The commentary on Surah [al-Jinn] is complete, and praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.
